Finnish satellite operator ICEYE made a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Italian rocket maker Avio on Tuesday, with the goal of creating an integrated European space and defense group.
The deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the US and China.
ICEYE said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news.
“Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said ICEYE, which intends to fund the offer with cash and debt.
ICEYE has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications.
“If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe‘s defense will rise to a new level,” said Finnish defense minister Antti Hakkanen.
Investments in Italy
State-backed ICEYE said it intends to invest an additional €1 billion in Italy over five years after the potential deal is completed, seeking to increase the launch cadence and expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket.
Avio‘s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which ICEYE said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price.
Speaking at an event in Helsinki, ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction.
The deal will need several regulatory approvals, including an official green light from the Italian government as Avio is seen as a strategic asset under Rome’s golden power rules.
The CEO of Italian defense group Leonardo, a key Avio shareholder with an 18% stake, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would examine it, in coordination with the government.
European Champion
The deal would pair Avio’s launch and propulsion capabilities with the satellite manufacturing, constellation operations and intelligence services of ICEYE, which was founded in 2014 and provides radar satellite imagery to Western governments and militaries.
“It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities… bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies.
The Finnish group said it intends to preserve Avio’s brand, retain its existing workforce and continue its planned investments in the United States.
As part of its push into the US defense market, Avio is building a manufacturing plant in Virginia, which it expects to complete in late 2028.
($1 = 0.9086 euros)

New U.S. export rules could slow Southeast Asia's data center boom by tightening access to advanced AI chips and targeting the region's role in providing computing power to Chinese companies.
According to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including those from Nvidia.
Facilities already serving large Chinese customers will have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions, the rule said.
The region has seen a surge in data center construction to house the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models.
U.S. restrictions on China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips have pushed Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent computing capacity in overseas data centers.
About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, according to October estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank.
The buildout has come under greater scrutiny as Washington presses ahead with the investigation into Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang left the company that he co-founded in 1993 after reports of several alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy who is believed to facilitate billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips into China.
The new restrictions will likely make building and operating these data centers "slower and costlier," said Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. The rules could undercut the business model of neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing — in the region, she said.
Operators are likely to face more rigorous regulatory and national security requirements, said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
Greater scrutiny over investment into these projects could also weigh on Asian economies that have benefited heavily from the region's data center build-out.
Who are most exposed?
Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions, analysts say, given the scale of capacity being built in Johor and the sector's reliance on Chinese customers.
More than half of Malaysia's data center capacity is in colocation facilities with Chinese firms accounting for "a sizeable share of these workloads," said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics.
Restricting access to overseas cloud facilities would weaken the commercial case for further expansion and ultimately weigh on investment from both Chinese and U.S. companies, Fahy said.

Thailand, which has more than 60 data centers operating and about 30 under construction, is also bracing for tighter scrutiny.

The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%.

Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday and Saturday, October 30 and 31, NCAA Division I Cross-Country Conference Championships took place in various locations across the United States. The competition was deep and fast, and we were treated to a preview of key matchups we will see at the national championships in a few weeks.
The Javelina 100 Mile also took place in Arizona’s McDowell Mountain Regional Park. Judging by the finish times — and despite heavy rains — it appears the front group of runners sprinted for a full 100 miles. In the women’s race, the victory was decided by a mere 56 seconds — a margin of victory that fills me with empathetic distress.
Then on Sunday, more than 61,000 runners took to the streets for the New York City Marathon. We watched epic throwdowns, including Sweden’s Andreas Almgren victory in his debut marathon, and American Jessica McClain came away with a brilliant runner-up finish over the final strides in the women’s race. These are exciting times to be a running fan.
The races themselves were great — the striving and struggling, camaraderie, mud, and the beauty of trying hard (1). But post-race interviews are always my favorite part of big race weekends. These interviews are often drenched in gratitude for good health and the opportunity to compete, for competitors, and for the people who supported their efforts along the way. We hear about families, friends, and volunteers. Athletes often speak in terms of “we” instead of “I.”
It is perhaps surprising that many of the biggest moments of a runner’s career are accompanied by expressions of gratitude. Instead of keeping the focus on themselves, they direct it to others. They win and are given a platform to speak. Then they use this platform to say, “Thank you (2).”
The Concept
Gratitude is a virtue of appreciation that involves recognizing that we have received some good or benefit. For runners, this “good” can mean the expertise of physical trainers, the company of running buddies, the encouragement of family members, or care from aid station volunteers. This recognition involves actions, thoughts, and emotions (3). Grateful people “behave in a thankful way towards their benefactors, but also have appropriate feelings of positive appreciation and regard for them (4).”
Gratitude involves a “to-for” structure: “We are thankful to someone for some gratuitous good (5).” This structure makes gratitude corrective of tendencies toward entitlement and thanklessness. Cheshire Calhoun writes that what makes gratitude a virtue is, in part, that it “corrects a tendency not to attend to the benefactor but instead simply to enjoy the benefit (6).” In other words, gratitude recognizes that others play a role in our flourishing and in the goods we possess. ‘You Absolutely Hate Your Money’: Clark Howard to Chase and Wells Fargo Savers
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Clark Howard was blunt on his November 16 show. If your savings sit at JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction), Bank of America (NYSE:BAC), Citigroup (NYSE:C) or Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC), the syndicated consumer money host told listeners, “you hate your money. You absolutely hate your money.”
He also gave the reason. “The biggest banks are going to pay you 1/100th of 1% on your savings,” he said, while “the US Treasury will pay you 5.51% on your savings.”
On $10,000, that works out to about $1 a year versus roughly $551. That gap is what you give up by leaving cash where it sits.
Howard Is Right About the Banks, and Treasury’s Numbers Back Him
My conclusion: Howard’s attack on big-bank savings rates holds up. His I bond pitch also works, but only for money you can lock away for at least a year. If you put your emergency cash into I bonds, you can’t get it back when an emergency hits.
TreasuryDirect confirms a 5.51%[1] rate on I bonds issued from November 1, 2026 to April 30, 2027. That rate combines a 1.4% fixed rate with a 2% semiannual inflation rate.
The fixed rate matters most, because Treasury says it never changes[1]. Bonds bought from July through October locked in just 0.9% fixed. Buy today and you lock in 1.4% above inflation for up to 30 years[1].
On $10,000, that extra half point adds about $50 a year on top of inflation.
The alternatives pay less. The FDIC’s national average 12-month CD yields 1.8%[2], and the 52-week Treasury bill recently yielded 4.55%. The I bond pays about 3 times the average CD.
Here is an example one-year comparison on $10,000. It assumes the I bond rate holds for the full year and ignores compounding:
Even after giving up roughly $138 in lost interest, the I bond still pays more than the average CD. The interest also escapes state and local income tax[1], and you can put off federal tax until you cash the bond in.
When You Need the Cash Decides Whether This Helps or Hurts
Treasury lets you cash in an I bond only after 12 months[1]. If you cash it in before five years, you lose the last 3 months of interest[1]. Howard said the same thing on air: “You have to own them for a minimum of a year.”
Say your transmission fails in month seven. Your I bond money is frozen, so the repair goes on a credit card that charges far more than the bond earns. Cash you might need belongs in an online savings account. Howard said those accounts can pay “as much as 400 times” what the megabanks pay.
Money you won’t touch for five years is a different story. There is no penalty, and you earn inflation plus 1.4%.
Remember that the 2% inflation piece looks back and resets every six months.
In the year through September, consumer prices rose about 3.7%, roughly double the Fed’s 2% goal. If inflation cools, the rate falls.
If the inflation piece drops to zero, you earn only the 1.4% fixed rate, which is less than today’s average CD. Howard has said he would consider cashing in I bonds in a very low inflation cycle.
His 30-year warning comes with a catch. “From that point forward, I earn nothing. Nothing. Not a penny,” he said. TreasuryDirect pays electronic bonds automatically[1] when they mature, so that risk mostly applies to old paper bonds.

Reddit (RDDT) stock closed at $94.48 on November 17, 2026, down 39.5% from its October 16 close. A drop that steep tempts anyone who liked the company at a higher price. The shares might be a bargain on a business that is still growing. Or they could be a warning that the underlying story has changed. The steepest single-day decline arrived right after Reddit reported its fiscal Q3 2026 results on October 29. So what did management tell investors on that call?
What Did Reddit Tell Investors On Its Q3 Call?
Search referral traffic, the visitors search engines send to Reddit, fell meaningfully in the third quarter, management said on the call. The decline sped up late in the quarter, management said. Management said the slide continued into early October. At that rate, it said, daily users could fall from 130 million by a low double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter. The shares lost 29.2% on October 30, the day after the call. That marked their largest one-day fall of the past year.
Management said on the call that the drop in search traffic appears to come from Google’s rollout of AI Mode. It said people still want Reddit, and Google is just not sending them there the way it used to. Management also said 80% of Reddit’s monetization happens in its app and among logged-in users. So the search warning on the call was about how many people reach Reddit, not about the ads it has already sold. On the same call, management guided fourth-quarter revenue growth below the third quarter’s pace.
Did Reddit’s Earlier Falls Of This Size Pay Off?
Since March 2024, Reddit stock has fallen more than 40% over 30 trading days three times. The latest, on November 2, 2026, came partway through this slide. The February 2026 drop is less than a year old. So only one has a full year behind it. In the 30 trading days to March 10, 2025, the shares fell 41.2% while the S&P 500 ETF fell 8.0%. A year after that date, they were 30.0% higher.
Collecting that gain meant sitting through a further fall first. At their lowest that year, the shares closed 19.0% below the March 10 price. The highest price came 192 days after the dip, about six months later. It stood 152.3% above the dip-date price. The February 2026 drop remains too recent to judge over a year, but the shares traded 14.0% higher six months on.
Reddit’s Business Is Still Growing Under The Drop
Revenue reached $895 million in fiscal Q3 2026, up 53.0% from a year earlier. Over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, Reddit kept 29.4% of revenue as operating income. In the twelve months before, it kept 13.8%. The company ended September with $3.03 billion in cash and short-term investments and $31.4 million of debt. The stock now costs 18.3 times the last twelve months’ earnings. The S&P 500 trades at 22.0 times earnings, so Reddit is cheaper than the market on that basis.

Management calls it the largest nonstate-owned refiner in the world. A stock like this can change how your whole portfolio behaves on the market’s good and bad days. How much depends on how much of it you hold. So does Exxon add to the market risk you already carry, or does it steady it?
Exxon Mobil Stock Has Moved Against The Market
In the year to November 17, 2026, Exxon Mobil stock tended to move against the S&P 500. On the average day when the index rose 0.67%, a $10,000 holding in Exxon lost about $33. On the average day when the index fell 0.63%, that holding gained about $66.
Exxon therefore steadied a market portfolio rather than adding to its risk. The stock recorded a beta of minus 0.56. Beta measures how far the stock moves when the index moves. A negative beta means the shares moved the other way on average.
You received this offset alongside wider swings in Exxon itself. Its volatility, how widely its daily moves spread over a year, stood at 27.1%, compared with 13.8% for the index. Exxon did not offset every bad day. On November 5, 2026, the index’s worst day of that year, Exxon fell 2.3% while the S&P 500 fell 4.4%.
You Have Been Paid Better For Exxon’s Swings
Over the five years since November 9, 2021, Exxon returned 24.6% a year including dividends. The S&P 500 returned 10.9% a year. Exxon’s annual volatility over those five years sat at 26.7%, against 17.2% for the index.
Dividing the return by the volatility reveals how much return each unit of swing earned. Exxon generated 0.92, against 0.63 for the S&P 500. The stock swung more than the market, but it paid you better for each swing.
Exxon Cannot Say When Fuel Markets Will Ease
On its October 30, 2026 earnings call, management said Middle East conflict had constrained supplies of crude, diesel and gasoline. Management said this lack of supply led to higher market prices. An analyst asked when refining margins would return to normal. Management said it had no line of sight on how the many variables would play out. It guessed it would take well through 2027, possibly longer.
Exxon’s results are tied to fuel markets that management itself cannot call. That uncertainty could keep the stock’s swings wide. The direction of those swings is less settled. Over the five years, Exxon’s daily moves had a weak positive correlation of 0.24 with the index. So moving against the market has not been its usual pattern. Exxon is expected to report in January 2027. The earnings of its Energy Products business are the number to watch.
If the past year’s pattern holds, Exxon may trim your portfolio’s gain a little on the next day the market rises, and offset part of the loss on the next day it falls. Own P&G Stock For Safety? Watch Bond Yields
Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?
Procter & Gamble stock has worked as a hiding place since mid-August. In the 63 trading days to Tuesday’s close, P&G rose 20.0%. Over the same days the S&P 500 fell 5.2%. The chip fund SMH fell 22.6%. So yes, P&G still hedges a tech sell-off. But the hedge now comes with a second bet attached.
Most of the talk about staples is about how pricey they look. This article looks at what a P&G holder now owns. Our price data shows a stock whose daily moves now run against chips and with Treasury bonds. That is not the same as a neutral safe place.
The key number is how P&G moves with the 10-year Treasury yield. Correlation measures how closely the daily moves of two prices go together. It runs from one (always in step) to minus one (always opposite). Over the last 63 trading days, P&G’s correlation with daily moves in the 10-year yield was -0.45. That is lower than the average of every year from 2015 to 2025. In plain words, P&G now tends to rise when yields fall. It tends to fall when yields rise.
The Staples Rally In One Table
The staples fund XLP closed at a record $92.60 on Monday, Nov 16. P&G itself is not at a record. It closed 4.4% below its Dec 2024 high. Still, over the last 63 trading days it rose more than any other staples name in the table below.

A Hedge Against Chips
Start with the part that works. XLP’s 63-day correlation with the chip fund was -0.50. P&G’s was -0.44. Both are below the average of every year from 2015 to 2025. Only 2.8% of XLP’s daily readings against chips since 2015 were lower.
The link to the wider market has faded too. P&G’s correlation with the S&P 500 was -0.06. Its yearly averages from 2015 to 2025 ran from +0.04 to +0.70. For now, P&G has been moving on its own path, away from tech.
The Bond Bet Inside The Hedge
Here is the part that is easy to miss. XLP’s correlation with daily moves in the 10-year yield was -0.44. That is below every yearly average from 2015 to 2025. IEF is a fund of Treasury bonds that mature in seven to ten years. XLP’s correlation with IEF was 0.45. That is higher than 98.6% of daily readings since 2015.
So staples now trade partly like bonds. A P&G holder owns a position that leans against tech and toward falling yields. If AI stocks recover while yields rise, we think both parts of that position could work against the holder at once.
This matters for anyone who also owns bonds for safety. The two holdings may now rise and fall on the same news. Our earlier piece asked whether dividend stocks are the new bonds. The correlation data says that, for staples right now, they partly are.
What 2022 Really Showed
The usual case for P&G points to 2022. In that calendar year P&G fell 7.3%. The S&P 500 fell 19.4%. P&G’s fall was less than half the market’s.
The path inside that year tells a different story. From its Jan 5 close to its Oct 11 close, P&G fell 24.3%. The S&P 500 fell 25.4% from its 2022 peak to its low. Measured that way, P&G fell almost as far as the market. That was also a year when bonds lost money. IEF fell 16.7% in 2022. Is Salesforce’s AI Sell-Off A Cash Bargain?
Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?
Salesforce stock fell 9.5% on Tuesday, Nov 17, to close at $194.52. It was the stock’s largest one-day fall since May 30, 2024, when it dropped 19.7%. The S&P 500 lost 1.0% the same day. ServiceNow fell 6.5% and Adobe fell 4.2%.
Why did it fall? MarketWatch reported that a series of technology outages left investors worried that software companies could be “particularly vulnerable” to AI misuse, citing an analyst. Invezz tied the fall to the same outages and to worries about software reliability and security. The Motley Fool said security jitters and fears that AI could replace software hit the whole group. Business Insider reported the same day that Salesforce has started cutting more jobs. No outlet showed that the job cuts moved the stock.
Most coverage focuses on the fear that AI could replace software. This article looks at cash. At Tuesday’s close, Salesforce traded at 10.5 times the free cash it produced over the past year. Free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. Measured the same way at each quarter end since 2010, only two readings were lower. So the stock is near its cheapest on cash in that record, but this is not a record low.
How Cheap Is Salesforce On Cash?
The price of 10.5 times cash flow equals a free cash flow yield of 9.5%. Across 67 quarter ends since 2010, the middle reading was 40.2 times. The lowest was just under 10 times, at the end of July 2026.
The stock got cheap quickly. It traded at 19.2 times cash flow at the end of October 2025. That fell to 13.8 times by the end of January 2026 and to 10.5 times by the end of April, a touch below Tuesday’s reading. The shares are down 26.6% this year. They closed 27.4% below their 52-week high and 47.1% below their record close of $367.87 on Dec 4, 2024. Tuesday’s close was the lowest since Aug 17.
One peer is cheaper than Salesforce on this measure and one is more expensive. Here is the same measure for the two software stocks that fell with it.
On this measure Salesforce is far cheaper than ServiceNow. Adobe is cheaper still, at 8.8 times. We looked at the same question for ServiceNow in how ServiceNow’s cash yield compares with Treasury bonds.
The Business Behind The Price
The low price is not because cash is shrinking. Free cash flow over the year to July 2026 was $15,154 million. That is 21.3% more than a year earlier. Revenue in the three months to July grew 10.8% from a year before.
Salesforce has also bought back a large amount of stock. Its diluted share count fell 14.7% in a year. It is now 18.2% below its January 2022 peak. Fewer shares means each remaining share owns more of the cash.
There is a cost to that. Buybacks over the four quarters to July totalled $35,070 million. That is 2.3 times the free cash flow of the same period. In the three months to April alone, Salesforce spent $27,248 million on its own stock. Total debt rose by $30,506 million over the year. It stood at $41,743 million at the end of July. So part of the buyback was paid with borrowed money, not with cash the business earned.

Who Really Pays For Nvidia’s $1.2 Trillion?
Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?
Analysts expect Nvidia to sell $1.2 trillion of chips a year by 2031. That is four times the $303 billion it sold over the four quarters to July, the base we use throughout. Adding Tuesday’s quarter, the four quarters to October come to about $362 billion.
Nvidia reported $115.8 billion of sales for the October quarter on Tuesday. It expects $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, for the January quarter. That quarter has an extra week, and the outlook assumes no data center compute sales to China.
So who pays? Someone has to find about $6 trillion of new spending a year. Anthropic’s IPO filing, amended Tuesday, points to a pool that big. It is the more than $40 trillion a year the world pays for knowledge work. AI would have to take over about 15% of it. Until then, investors are paying. If you own Nvidia, or an S&P 500 fund, you own this bet.
Where Does Nvidia’s Money Come From?
Nvidia sells to the companies building AI data centers. They include Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle and CoreWeave. With a few others, they took in $2.04 trillion over the last four quarters. About $37 of every $100 went into capital spending, mostly data centers. Nvidia’s sales equal about 40% of that spending. So roughly $1 of every $7 the buyers take in reaches Nvidia.
So $900 billion more for Nvidia means about $6 trillion more for its buyers. That is the step from $303 billion to $1.2 trillion. At $1 in $7, the buyers would need about $6 trillion of new revenue every year, on top of today’s $2 trillion. That is almost a fifth of the $33 trillion US economy.

The company is investing in pipelines, power generation and carbon storage, while finding ways to get more value from its existing assets.
The strategy comes at a time when California faces growing electricity demand and continues to rely on oil and natural gas. Management believes the company's land, production facilities and energy infrastructure give it an advantage in serving both markets. Its third-quarter 2026 results show how the company is balancing these growth plans with cost control and shareholder returns.
CRC Expands Pipeline Network, Sharpens California Focus

Cardinals Box Up Thanksgiving Meals for Military Veterans
Hundreds of military families in Missouri and Illinois will be receiving Thanksgiving meal kits next week, thanks to a partnership between the Cardinals and the St. Louis Area Foodbank.
A couple of dozen Cardinal employees spent their Wednesday morning packing 625 boxes with green beans, corn, apple sauce, stuffing, and macaroni and cheese. Each box is intended to feed a family of four (2,500 people total), and will also include one more side dish – a note of gratitude handwritten by someone in the Cardinals front office.

"Being able to partner with the St. Louis Cardinals, which is such a historic organization, to give back to not only the community but to veterans specifically, just means the world to us," said Jordan Casey, Product Sourcing Project Manager for the St. Louis Area Foodbank as Cardinals employees manned three long tables and quickly assembled and stacked the boxes. "The support, getting the employees to come out like this, is inspiring. And it will kind of be a surprise to our VA partners that they’ll be receiving these Thanksgiving boxes."
The process was expected to take four hours, but Cardinals volunteers came out in such abundance that it was finished in half that time.
The St. Louis Area Foodbank covers 26 counties in Missouri and Illinois, and there is a tremendous need for its services, Casey noted, adding: "In those counties, there are enough people facing food insecurity to fill Busch Stadium 10 times."

ExxonMobil's relatively small dividend increase was actually a big achievement.

Companies don't usually initiate regular dividend payments until they have grown to a point where they have sufficient reliable income with which to do so. I believe AI poses a significant market risk, but I'm not selling my technology stocks.
By Reuben Gregg Brewer –
Key Points
- I vividly remember the dot-com bubble and its aftermath.
- I bought IBM and Texas Instruments before the AI bubble got underway.
- I'm not changing my investment approach because I'm concerned that there's a market correction on the way.
The number one thing I don't want to do, at any time and for any reason, is change my long-term investment approach to fit the current market zeitgeist. It is hard to stick to a long-term plan, especially when you believe there's a material risk of a stock market correction. But history shows that while corrections come and go, the market has always resumed its upward march.
This is why, despite my concerns about an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, I'm not selling either of my two technology stocks: International Business Machines (IBM -1.11%) and Texas Instruments (TXN -1.16%). Here's a deeper dive into why sticking to my dividend-centric investment approach trumps the risk of the AI bubble bursting.
There will be a bear market
I don't know when it will arrive, but I know with 100% certainty that there will be another bear market. And if history is any guide, a bull market will follow, eventually pushing the market to new all-time highs. That's what history shows, and you just have to look at a graph of the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.23%) to prove to yourself that buying and holding is a pretty good investment plan.
That said, I am a dividend investor with a value focus. My preference is to buy companies with long histories of dividend growth when they have historically high yields. I believe those two facts indicate a good business and an attractive valuation. That's how I came across IBM and Texas Instruments. At this point, IBM's dividend streak is up to 31 years, while Texas Instruments' is at 23 years.
I bought both stocks before the artificial intelligence trade took off, so my decision to jump aboard had nothing to do with that technology. I like IBM because it has an over 100-year history of adapting to the world around it, with a focus on serving business customers. I'm fond of Texas Instruments because it makes boring computer chips that go into just about every electronic device. I would fully expect the two companies to be involved in AI and, in fact, I would be upset if they didn't attempt to benefit from this still-emerging technology in some way.

he Trump administration is launching a new effort to combat a surge in crypto fraud and other cybercrimes targeting Americans, attacks that largely come from criminal networks located overseas.
The newly formed Threat Disruption Center will operate as a technology resource and collaboration hub for the Homeland Security Task Force, the administration said Wednesday. The center, which is comprised of more than 30 federal agencies and more than 440 state and local partners, will provide tools to address complaints from scam victims and map the networks behind the criminal operations.
The effort is being established pursuant to an executive order Trump issued in March that directed government agencies to develop a response to cybercrime and fraud that are “draining American families of their life savings, stealing the benefits of years of work and destroying the lives of our youth.”
The center will “identify victims, trace victim funds back to bad actors, identify the crypto wallets utilized both by those bad actors, and then ultimately try to identify other victims,” said Eric Weindorf, deputy director of the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center.
As part of the new effort, the government is paying TRM Labs Inc. about $95 million to provide technical support, including an artificial intelligence platform that will serve as its primary investigative tool. More than 60 TRM employees are working on the project.
“We’re looking at how can we use AI to triage victim reports in more near real time and surface opportunities where very quick action on behalf of the government could return funds to victims,” said Esteban Castaño, chief executive of TRM.
Victims in the US and abroad told the Federal Bureau of Investigation that they lost almost $21 billion to cybercrime last year, a roughly 25% surge from the previous year. Crypto-related losses accounted for more than half of that total.
The surge in fraud has posed a challenge to local law enforcement officials, in part because much of it originates overseas. It is also nearly impossible to retrieve stolen funds, which are often converted into cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin or Tether.
An outlier is the Brooklyn District Attorney’s office, which three years ago established the Virtual Currency Unit to respond to an onslaught of fraud. Run by assistant district attorney Alona Katz, the unit recently seized and disrupted more than 240 crypto-fraud websites and 112 computer servers controlled by an Eastern European fraud group, which the Brooklyn DA’s office said was “one of the biggest operational cyber disruptions undertaken by a local prosecutors’ office.”
“The Brooklyn DAs office is one of the country’s pioneers in going after these threats,” Castaño said. The Threat Disruption Center will apply the approach “across the federal government,” he said.
The government awarded the one-year agreement to TRM in July without putting it up for competitive bidding. One of TRM’s rivals, Chainalysis, sued the Trump administration, alleging that the contract awarding process was “arbitrary, capricious and unreasonable.” The lawsuit was dismissed in September.

The company’s latest report, in its eighth year, found that ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world with ‘admin’, ‘12345678’, ‘123456789’, and ‘1234’ rounding out the top five most used passwords totaling more than 15,000,000 users.
The findings suggest users favor simple, easy-to-remember passwords making them all the more vulnerable to cracking.
Analysis revealed that pop culture informs passwords globally, making them easy to crack in seconds. For example, ‘Lebron0319’ tops the list as the most used password in the sports category within the current decade. A top television referenced-password is ‘squidgamethebest’, while ‘Covid-19’ and ‘Covid@19’ were top contenders in the ‘other’ category.
NordPass recommends using strong passwords and passphrases, indicating that “a strong password should contain at least 15 characters and use a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special symbols.”
Passphases, a sequences of words, may also be used to create a strong password.
Keeping passwords unique to each account is also a way to increase security.
In addition, it is recommended to check account passwords regularly to maintain security and switch on multi-factor identification to add an extra layer of protection.
The password manager says passkey technology may be the solution to the password manager problem. They define passkeys as” a passwordless authentication credential that uses cryptographic keys instead of character-based passwords. It links your identity to your device, allowing you to sign in with built-in biometrics, such as a fingerprint, face scan, or device PIN. Because the private key never leaves your device, passkeys eliminate the need to remember or type passwords, offering faster, simpler, and more secure authentication.”
The benefits of passkeys is that they:
-
Are strong by default, ensuring robust security
-
Eliminate the need to create complex strings of characters or commit them to memory
-
Are unique per-service, preventing the risk of reuse across multiple accounts
-
Enhancing security, since the private key associated with passkeys remains confidential
-
Offer high resistance to phishing , brute-force attacks , and other cyber threats

Sens. Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell announced the agreement Tuesday at a demonstration on the lawn outside the Capitol building. A group representing families of the 67 people killed when an American Airlines flight collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Washington, D.C., on Jan. 29, 2025, organized the event.
“When military aircraft fly in the same airspace, they must meet the same standards as everyone else,” said Cantwell, a Democrat representing Washington state.

Hamaad Raza lost his wife, Asra Hussain, in the crash. He said his wife was terrified of flying but she had to for work, so he would always reassure her that she would be safe. Since then, he has learned about the locator systems that the airline pilots didn’t have that night which the National Transportation Safety Board has been recommending for decades.
“Every time she was scared, I would reassure her. That she had nothing to worry about. I did this because I truly believed it,” Raza said. “Like most people, I had heard that air travel was the safest form of transportation. And because of the industry’s track record, I had blind trust in the American aviation system. What I did not realize at the time was this crash was a ticking time bomb, and it was inevitable.”
On the night of the collision, the Army helicopter flew without the key ADS-B Out system that broadcasts an aircraft’s location turned on because of security concerns, even though it was only on a training flight.
Any aircraft flying in crowded airspace is already required to have the ADS-B Out system that broadcasts its location but isn’t required to have the complementary ADS-B In systems that show pilots where nearby aircraft are flying. Some airlines have invested in the technology in newer planes and private pilots often use a portable receiver to see the locations on an iPad.
“Pilots can’t avoid what we can’t see,” said Capt. Jason Ambrosi, who leads the Air Line Pilots Association union. He said Congress must require these systems on both military and civilian aircraft because the Federal Aviation Administration hasn’t. “Everyone in shared airspace must be seen. Period.”

As of November 18, 2026, the 52-week Treasury bill yielded 4.59%. The 26-week bill yielded 4.46%, the 13-week 4.26%, and the 4-week 4.00%. The longest bill pays the most, and it pays more than some of the best-known dividend stocks. For a saver at or near retirement, the real question is whether a stock’s payout is worth giving up a rate the government promises to pay.
How a Treasury Bill Pays You and When Its Rate Resets
A Treasury bill is a loan to the U.S. government maturing in one year or less. You buy it for less than its face value, and when it matures, the Treasury pays you the full face value. The difference is your interest. Bills have no coupon and send you nothing along the way. According to the IRS, bills generally have a 4-, 8-, 13-, 26-, or 52-week maturity period and are issued at a discount in $100 increments.
The rate is set at auction on the day you buy. Hold the bill to maturity, and its income is fixed. When it matures, you get cash back, and to keep earning you have to roll into a new bill at whatever rate the market sets on that day. The 4.59% figure is really just a snapshot.
It goes only to bills bought at that rate. Someone rolling 4-week bills gets a new rate 13 times a year, and someone rolling 52-week bills gets one once a year. The figure stays locked for neither.
Bills carry three risks that savers often miss:
- Reinvestment risk. If rates fall, every rollover pays less. Income that looked steady can shrink quickly.
- Price risk. You can sell a bill through a broker before it matures, but if rates have risen since you bought it, you may get back less than you paid. Holding to maturity avoids this.
- Inflation risk. The face value is a fixed dollar amount, so rising prices eat into what it buys.
The government’s backing has limits too. The full faith and credit of the United States backs repayment of face value at maturity. The guarantee leaves out the price you’d get selling early, the rate on your next rollover, or what inflation does to your buying power. Bills also pay no monthly income. Getting regular checks in retirement requires staggering several maturities.
Dividend Safety Matters More Than Dividend Size
Each investment has a weakness the other lacks. A dividend can be cut. The board decides on each payment and can lower or suspend it at any time. A Treasury bill’s payout is a legal obligation fixed when you buy. A dividend can grow. A board can raise it year after year. A bill’s income changes only when rates change, and then only when you roll over. That makes dividend safety the starting point for any comparison, ahead of yield.
